takeaway: Hyperkalaemia (e.g. after massive blood transfusion) causes peaked T waves, reduced P waves and a broad QRS; it can end in arrhythmia and asystole.

question.text: After several units of blood following a road traffic collision, which ECG change would you expect in hyperkalaemia?
question.say: After several units of blood following a road traffic collision, which ECG change would you expect in hyperkalaemia?

lines.text: This patient has had several units of blood after a crash. Massive transfusion is a recognised cause of hyperkalaemia.
Meet the muscular potassium banana, overflowing from its cup. High potassium makes the cardiac cell membranes hyperpolarised.
On the monitor, the T waves rise like tall circus tents. Peaked T waves are the classic ECG sign.
Look underneath: the P waves become small and reduced.
So of the options, peaked T waves is the change you would expect.
